words.definition: a vertical section through soil showing distinct horizons from the surface to parent material
words.example: A soil profile reveals changes in organic matter, colour and texture with depth.

words.definition: the upper mineral soil horizon, usually rich in organic matter and biological activity
words.example: Most crop roots and soil organisms are concentrated in topsoil.

words.definition: the soil layer beneath topsoil, often containing accumulated minerals and less organic matter
words.example: Clay and iron compounds may accumulate in the subsoil.

words.definition: the underlying geological material from which much of a soil develops
words.example: Granite and limestone produce soils with different chemical properties because of their parent material.

words.definition: dark, relatively stable organic material formed by decomposition of plant and animal remains
words.example: Humus improves nutrient retention and soil structure.

words.definition: the relative proportions of sand, silt and clay particles in soil
words.example: Soil texture strongly influences drainage and water retention.

words.definition: the largest common mineral particle size in soil, producing relatively rapid drainage
words.example: Sandy soils usually have large pores and low water-holding capacity.

words.definition: intermediate-sized mineral particles that feel smooth when moist
words.example: Silt-rich soils can be fertile but may erode easily.

words.definition: very fine mineral particles with high surface area and strong water and nutrient retention
words.example: Clay soils can hold nutrients but may drain slowly.

words.definition: the arrangement of soil particles into aggregates and pore spaces
words.example: Good soil structure supports aeration, infiltration and root growth.

words.definition: the proportion of soil volume occupied by pores
words.example: Organic matter can increase soil porosity.

words.definition: the ease with which water or air moves through soil
words.example: Sandy soil generally has higher permeability than compacted clay.

words.definition: a measure of the acidity or alkalinity of soil
words.example: Soil pH influences nutrient availability to plants.

words.definition: the capacity of soil to supply nutrients and suitable conditions for plant growth
words.example: Adding compost can improve soil fertility.

words.definition: the ability of soil particles to retain and exchange positively charged nutrient ions
words.example: Clay and humus often give soils a high cation exchange capacity.

words.definition: carbon-based material in soil derived from living and once-living organisms
words.example: Soil organic matter improves water retention and nutrient cycling.

words.definition: accumulation of soluble salts in soil to levels that reduce plant growth
words.example: Poor drainage under irrigation can cause salinization.

words.definition: removal and transport of soil by water, wind or human activity
words.example: Bare fields are especially vulnerable to soil erosion during heavy rain.

words.definition: land degradation in dry regions resulting from climatic variation and human pressures
words.example: Overgrazing and drought can contribute to desertification.

words.definition: management practices designed to protect soil from erosion, degradation and fertility loss
words.example: Contour farming and cover crops are methods of soil conservation.

words.definition: agriculture mainly producing food for the farmer's household or local consumption rather than sale
words.example: Subsistence farming often relies heavily on family labour.

words.definition: agriculture primarily producing crops or livestock for sale in markets
words.example: Commercial farming may use specialized machinery and large areas of land.

words.definition: farming that uses high inputs of labour, capital, fertilizer or energy per unit area
words.example: Greenhouse vegetable production is a form of intensive agriculture.

words.definition: farming using relatively low inputs per unit area over large areas
words.example: Cattle grazing on large rangelands is typically extensive agriculture.

words.definition: cultivation of crops on land that is regularly ploughed or otherwise prepared
words.example: Wheat production is a common form of arable farming.

words.definition: agriculture focused mainly on raising grazing livestock
words.example: Sheep ranching is a form of pastoral farming.

words.definition: a system that combines crop production with livestock raising
words.example: Mixed farming can recycle manure from animals onto crop fields.

words.definition: large-scale cultivation of a single crop species or variety
words.japanese: 単一栽培・モノカルチャー
words.example: Monoculture can simplify harvesting but may increase vulnerability to pests.

words.definition: cultivation of several crop species together in the same area
words.example: Polyculture can increase habitat diversity within farmland.

words.definition: planned sequence of different crops grown on the same land across seasons or years
words.example: Legumes in a crop rotation can improve soil nitrogen.

words.definition: land management that deliberately combines trees with crops or livestock
words.japanese: アグロフォレストリー
words.example: Agroforestry can provide shade, reduce erosion and diversify farm income.

words.definition: agriculture that limits synthetic fertilizers and pesticides and emphasizes ecological management
words.example: Organic farming often relies on compost, crop rotation and biological pest control.

words.definition: use of sensors, data and targeted technology to apply farm inputs more accurately
words.example: GPS-guided fertilizer application is an example of precision agriculture.

words.definition: construction of stepped fields on slopes to reduce runoff and soil erosion
words.example: Terracing can make steep land more suitable for cultivation.

words.definition: a substance added to soil or crops to supply plant nutrients
words.example: Excess fertilizer can increase yield but also contribute to water pollution.

words.definition: a substance used to kill or control organisms considered harmful to crops or livestock
words.example: Repeated pesticide use can select for resistant pest populations.

words.definition: a cultivated plant whose genetic material has been deliberately altered using biotechnology
words.example: A genetically modified crop may be engineered for pest resistance.

words.definition: reliable physical and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food
words.example: Drought, conflict and high prices can reduce food security.

words.definition: the distance food travels from production to consumption, sometimes used as an indicator of transport impact
words.example: Locally produced food may have fewer food miles, although total impact depends on production methods.

words.definition: food production that maintains productivity while protecting soils, water, biodiversity and long-term livelihoods
words.example: Reduced tillage and efficient irrigation can support sustainable agriculture.
